newsitem.title: USA: N.C. pork group says non-hog firms threaten water.
newsitem.headline: N.C. pork group says non-hog firms threaten water.

text.p: North Carolina pork producers said the industry would agree to a one-year halt on building new large hog farms if similar moratoriums were applied to other industries that threaten the state's water supply.
"There are multiple sources of water quality problems in this state," said Walter Cherry, executive director of the North Carolina Pork Council.

On Tuesday, Representative Richard Morgan introduced a House Bill 515 bill in the state legislature that proposed a one-year moratorium on construction or expansion of any swine farm or waste lagoon in the state.

Cherry said the Pork Council now opposes a moratorium on new contruction but would agree to one if other industries were included. He said recent studies have shown agriculture fertilizer and waste from residential septic tanks have contributed greatly to water contamination in the state.

Also, he said the Pork Council, which represents the state's 5,000 producers, would like the bill revised to allow construction of swine operations if the owners implement new technology for odor control and waste management.
North Carolina ranks second in U.S. pork production, behind Iowa, and as of March 1, had about 8.45 million hogs being readied for slaughter.

Along with the one-year moratorium, Morgan's bill would establish minimum distances between large hog operations and schools, parks, recreation areas, hospitals, and homes. Also, it would require a quarter-mile separation between hog farms and any surface water such as ponds, streams or lakes.
Cherry said the bill's quarter-mile setback requirement from surface water would essentially halt construction of hog farms because of the numerous ponds, lakes and streams.
"If that setback remains in HB 515, it will make it illegal to build a hog farm in this state," he said.
